ts6_blackstone.topic: William E. Blackstone and the Blackstone Memorials of 1891 and 1916

claims.text: Blackstone was born 6 October 1841 in Adams, New York, converted at a Methodist revival aged 11, settled in Oak Park, Illinois, in 1870 and prospered in building and property; he died 7 November 1935.

Jesus Is Coming was published in 1878 under the initials W.E.B. and translated into over 40 languages; Moorhead calls it 'the most important early book on premillennialism' and Blackstone 'an ardent supporter of dispensational premillennialism'.

Blackstone founded the Chicago Hebrew Mission (1887; renamed two years later; today Life in Messiah), an evangelistic mission to Jews, and organised the Conference on the Past, Present, and Future of Israel, 24–25 November 1890, First Methodist Episcopal Church, Chicago.
Secretary of State Blaine introduced Blackstone to President Harrison on 5 March 1891; Harrison 'received the Memorial kindly and promised to give it his consideration'.

The memorial asked 'What shall be done for the Russian Jews?', 'Where shall 2,000,000 of such poor people go?', and 'Why not give Palestine back to them again?', calling Palestine 'an inalienable possession from which they were expelled by force' and invoking the Treaty of Berlin (Bulgaria to the Bulgarians, Servia to the Servians).
The memorial asked the President and Secretary of State to secure 'an International Conference to consider the condition of the Israelites, and their claims to Palestine'.

Signature count disputed: 413 (Moorhead p. 791) vs 431 (Wikipedia). Named signers include John D. Rockefeller, J. Pierpont Morgan, Speaker Thomas Reed, Cyrus McCormick, D. L. Moody, Chief Justice Melville Fuller and William McKinley; Wheaton describes signers as religious (Christian and Jewish), civic, business and political leaders.

Wheaton archive: the memorial was received politely with no other official response; it may have influenced American protests to Russia. Moorhead: Harrison's December 1891 message to Congress did not name Blackstone but Feinstein read it as a reaction to the appeal.
Blackstone first saw Jewish return as a step toward Jewish conversion; at Clune's Auditorium, Los Angeles, 27 January 1918 he told the audience God's plan for the Jews was repentance and conversion.

Nathan Straus wrote to Blackstone that Brandeis 'agrees with me that you are the father of Zionism, as your work antedates Herzl' (dated 8 May 1916 in Moorhead; 16 May 1916 in Wikipedia); Brandeis wrote on 28 May 1916 that the document 'is destined to become of historical significance'.

The 1916 memorial gained the endorsement of the Presbyterian Church U.S.A. General Assembly and 82 individual endorsements (Chicago, Los Angeles, New York, Ithaca); addenda from Los Angeles Methodists, Los Angeles Baptists and Chicago Methodists survive at Wheaton.

Presentation of the second memorial is disputed: 'unofficially' to Wilson in May 1916 (Wheaton); privately in May 1917 (Wikipedia); never formally presented, partly because the British disliked its international character, with Wilson's approval reaching Stephen Wise on 31 August 1918 (Moorhead p. 799).
Blackstone sent Herzl a Bible with prophecies marked; Moorhead notes there is no proof Blackstone influenced Herzl.

ts6_balfour.topic: Balfour, Lloyd George, Wingate: Christian Zionism among the motives

claims.text: Philip Alexander: 'A crucial ingredient in Balfour's Zionism [may have been] his Christian belief'; Donald Lewis (2010) is the most persuasive advocate of the Christian-formation thesis; the article states both Balfour and Lloyd George 'were influenced by Christian Zionism'.
Kessler: Lloyd George's Baptist upbringing predisposed him to Weizmann's vision; he felt more at home with Palestinian place names than with Western Front sites.

War Cabinet minutes of 31 October 1917 record Balfour's view that a declaration would allow 'extremely useful propaganda both in Russia and America'; Robert Cecil wrote 'I do not think it is possible to exaggerate the international power of the Jews'; Schneer and Renton describe officials' belief in Jewish power.
Schneer calls the Declaration 'the highly contingent product of a tortuous process'; Chapman's one criticism is that the book has no discussion of the religious beliefs of Balfour and Lloyd George.

In secret 1937 testimony to the Peel Commission (released 2017, found by Oren Kessler), Lloyd George said the 'friendliness or hostility of the Jewish race might make a considerable difference' to the war and that Jews were 'a dangerous people to quarrel with, but ... a very helpful people if you can get them on your side'.
Kessler describes Lloyd George as 'Judeophobe and philo-Semite, militarist and appeaser, Zionist champion and Hitler enthusiast'.
Wingate's father became a committed member of the Plymouth Brethren; the children memorised Scripture daily; Wingate saw a Jewish state as a religious duty.

Haining approved the Special Night Squads in June 1938; after the killing of Chaim Sturman in September 1938 Wingate led a reprisal on Beisan's Arab quarter; Tom Segev called him 'quite mad, and perhaps a sadist, too'; Michael Oren disputed Segev.

Wingate was transferred to Britain in May 1939, his superiors judging him compromised by his Zionist involvement; he died on 24 March 1944 in a B-25 crash in Manipur; the Wingate Institute, Yemin Orde and Kikar Wingate are named for him.

ts6_committees.topic: The American Palestine Committee, the Christian Council on Palestine, the ACPC, and Truman's 'I am Cyrus'

claims.text: The Christian Council on Palestine was founded at an all-day meeting on 14 December 1942 at the Pennsylvania Hotel, New York; Henry A. Atkinson chaired; 30 people are listed present, including Reinhold Niebuhr, Bishop Francis J. McConnell, Bishop James Cannon Jr., Carl H. Voss, Rabbi Philip S. Bernstein and Emanuel Neumann; W. F. Albright was absent through illness.

Officers: Atkinson chairman, Howard B. Warren vice-chairman, John W. Bradbury honorary vice-chairman, Niebuhr treasurer. Policy point I: 'committed to the establishment of a Jewish commonwealth in Palestine'; procedure: 'an autonomous committee working in cooperation with the American Palestine Committee'; funding by 'Popular subscription' in cooperation with the APC.
At the meeting Neumann explained the work of the American Palestine Committee; a February 1943 Neumann statement in the same file calls the Council 'hundreds of prominent Christian Clergymen'.

Voss and Rausch credit Atkinson as founder and Niebuhr's leadership in founding the CCP in 1942; it was 'composed, as planned, almost entirely of Christian ministers'; the ACPC from 1946 carried on the combined work, claimed 'more than 20,000 Christian leaders', was mostly Protestant, and wound down in the late 1950s and early 1960s as financial support shrank. Voss was a founder and first executive director of the ACPC.

Hummel, reviewing Goldman (2018): Niebuhr was the 'most outspoken postwar Protestant supporter of Israel', backing a Jewish state on moral and realist grounds, not literal prophecy; Goldman traces a continuous Protestant 'Cyrus' tradition from covenant theology (Increase Mather, Jonathan Edwards).

The ACPC became the leading American Christian lobby for a Jewish state and coordinated opposition to UN efforts to internationalise Jerusalem; the pastor J. Frank Norris preached support for Zionism as a Christian duty and wrote to Truman in 1947 and 1948.

Truman joined a Baptist church in Kansas City at 18; Merkley writes that his Sunday School teachers taught that someone would be called to be a second Cyrus; at the Jewish Theological Seminary in November 1953, introduced by Eddie Jacobson as the man who helped create Israel, he replied 'I am Cyrus. I am Cyrus.' (Merkley gives no source for the account).
Merkley concludes 'personal commitment tipped the balance' and calls Truman and Wilson Christian Zionists; Judis calls the picture of unwavering support 'dead wrong'.

Spector (as reported by Tablet, 2008): Genesis 12:3 is the reason most often cited; about five million evangelicals are premillennial dispensationalists, and 'most Christian Zionists don't actually base their support for Israel on a catastrophic end-times scenario'.

claims.text: Audit re-fetch: Wheaton archive quotes the 1891 memorial: 'Let us restore them to the land of which they were so cruelly despoiled by our Roman ancestors'; says the May 1916 unofficial presentation to Wilson may have influenced Wilson's favourable response to the Balfour Declaration.

Audit re-fetch: Wikipedia (Blackstone Memorial): 431 signers; Straus 16 May 1916 'perfectly infatuated'; Brandeis asked for a second memorial for Wilson; endorsements from the Presbyterian Church and 'most of the mainstream American Protestant movement'; presented privately May 1917 and strongly influenced Wilson.

Audit re-fetch: Wikipedia (Blackstone): 4 November 1887 meeting at Benjamin Douglass's offices, Blackstone first superintendent; Nov 1890 conference attended by Orthodox Jewish and Protestant leaders, not Reform; called on the powers to 'give Palestine to the Zionists' and passed resolutions of sympathy for Russian Jews; refugees not admitted by Europe or the US.
Audit re-fetch: Wikipedia (Balfour Declaration) does not list Suez/India among motives and does not call the 'world Jewry' belief antisemitic; Schneer describes stereotypical thinking about Jews.

Audit re-fetch: Wikipedia (Wingate): he often returned to Ein Harod 'because of its association with the biblical judge Gideon'; after speaking publicly for a Jewish state on leave in Britain, superiors removed him, judging he was 'promoting his own agenda rather than that of the army or the government'.

Audit re-fetch: CCP minutes: W. Russell Bowie opened with prayer; Bishops McConnell, Cannon and Herbert Welch present; Carl H. Voss of Pittsburgh; Albright's telegram cited sudden illness; policy point I relates the commonwealth to 'an over-all settlement in the post-war era'.
Audit re-fetch: Voss and Rausch date the APC to 1931 and note Niebuhr's membership 'from the early 1930s'.

Audit re-fetch: Merkley: Truman 'maintained membership in a Baptist church throughout his life'; 'we must assume that personal commitment tipped the balance'; recognised Israel 'within hours', 'defying the uniform advice of his State and War Departments'; no source for the 1953 exchange.
